title: Week 12 · Lesson 35: Endocrine Pharmacology I — Diabetes Medications, Insulin & Safe Glycemic Care
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 12 — Lesson 35: Endocrine Pharmacology I — Diabetes Medications, Insulin & Safe Glycemic Care

FNP-level goal: Select glucose-lowering therapy by connecting glycemic goals to cardiovascular, kidney, heart-failure, weight, hypoglycemia, cost, and patient-safety priorities.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why diabetes medication selection is person-centered rather than based only on A1C.
  • Compare major medication classes by mechanism, benefit, adverse effects, and monitoring needs.
  • Recognize when insulin is needed and how to reduce insulin-related harm.
  • Identify hypoglycemia, hyperglycemic crisis, and medication-related red flags requiring urgent escalation.
  • Build a safe follow-up, sick-day, and medication-reconciliation plan.

Part 1 — The Diabetes Medication Question

Do not begin with, “Which drug lowers A1C the most?” Begin with:

What does this individual patient need to achieve, and what harm must I avoid?

Medication choice can be influenced by glycemic severity, symptoms, type of diabetes, ASCVD, heart failure, CKD, obesity, hypoglycemia risk, pregnancy potential, liver disease, age, cognitive function, injection ability, access, food security, and patient preference.

For many patients, glycemic care and cardiometabolic risk reduction are inseparable. A medication may be chosen for glucose lowering, heart-failure benefit, kidney benefit, cardiovascular benefit, weight effect, or a combination of these goals.

Part 2 — Individualized Goals and Therapeutic Inertia

Glycemic goals are individualized. A goal that is appropriate for a healthy younger adult may not be appropriate for an older patient with frailty, recurrent hypoglycemia, limited life expectancy, or high treatment burden.

At the same time, “individualization” must not become therapeutic inertia. Persistent symptomatic hyperglycemia, repeated high readings, or worsening complications requires an active reassessment of diagnosis, adherence, barriers, regimen effectiveness, and escalation plan.

Part 3 — Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Require Different Medication Logic

Type 1 diabetes involves absent or near-absent beta-cell insulin production. Insulin is essential. Omitting insulin can lead to ketosis and life-threatening DKA.

Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell dysfunction. Noninsulin medications may be appropriate, but some patients need insulin—especially with symptomatic severe hyperglycemia, catabolic features, hyperglycemic crisis, or inadequate control despite an individualized regimen.

Never apply a type 2 medication algorithm to a possible type 1 diabetes presentation without urgently clarifying the diagnosis and safety needs.

Part 4 — Metformin

Metformin primarily reduces hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity. It remains a commonly used, effective, and relatively inexpensive medication when no other comorbidity or treatment goal drives a different initial approach.

Key reasoning points include gastrointestinal tolerance, kidney function, risk of dehydration or acute illness, vitamin B12 concerns with long-term use in appropriate contexts, and the patient’s ability to take the medication consistently. During serious acute illness, hypoxia, dehydration, or kidney-function deterioration, reassess medication safety according to current guidance and the clinical situation.

Part 5 — GLP-1 Receptor and Dual GIP/GLP-1-Based Therapies

GLP-1-based therapies enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress inappropriate glucagon signaling, slow gastric emptying, and increase satiety. Some agents have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in appropriate patients; effects on weight can also be clinically meaningful.

Important safety and counseling issues include nausea, vomiting, dehydration risk, delayed gastric emptying, gallbladder symptoms, pancreatitis evaluation when clinically suspected, retinopathy monitoring in selected higher-risk patients, and medication-specific contraindications or warnings. A patient with severe persistent abdominal pain or dehydration needs clinical assessment rather than routine dose escalation.

Part 6 — SGLT2 Inhibitors

SGLT2 inhibitors reduce renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose excretion. In selected patients they have demonstrated heart-failure and kidney benefits that may influence therapy even when A1C alone does not explain the choice.

Because the mechanism promotes glycosuria and an osmotic effect, assess volume status, genital/urinary symptoms, kidney function, concurrent diuretics, and risk of dehydration. Educate patients about sick-day considerations and symptoms of ketoacidosis. Ketoacidosis can occur with less dramatic glucose elevation than patients expect; nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dyspnea, or altered mentation in a susceptible patient requires urgent evaluation.

Part 7 — Sulfonylureas and Hypoglycemia Risk

Sulfonylureas increase insulin secretion independent of the current glucose level. They can lower glucose effectively but raise hypoglycemia risk, particularly with missed meals, kidney impairment, older age, alcohol exposure, medication interactions, or an overly complex regimen.

If a new medication with lower hypoglycemia risk is added, reassess whether insulin or a secretagogue dose needs adjustment. More glucose-lowering drugs do not automatically mean a safer regimen.

Part 8 — DPP-4 Inhibitors and Other Oral Therapies

DPP-4 inhibitors prolong endogenous incretin activity and generally have a lower hypoglycemia risk when not combined with insulin or a secretagogue. They have a more modest glucose-lowering role for many patients. Selection still depends on kidney function, heart-failure history for particular agents, cost, and the rest of the regimen.

A key medication-reconciliation principle: combining a DPP-4 inhibitor with a GLP-1–based therapy is generally not useful for additional glucose lowering and adds complexity. Review mechanisms before adding therapy.

Part 9 — Thiazolidinediones: Fluid Matters

Thiazolidinediones improve insulin sensitivity but can cause fluid retention and weight gain. In a patient with edema, symptomatic heart failure, or high risk of fluid-related decompensation, this mechanism matters.

When a patient has new weight gain, dyspnea, edema, or orthopnea after a medication change, do not assume it is simply “diabetes getting worse.” Consider medication effect, heart failure, kidney disease, dietary sodium, and other contributors.

Part 10 — Insulin: Replacement, Not Failure

Insulin is required in type 1 diabetes and can be necessary or highly effective in type 2 diabetes. Starting insulin is not a moral failure or evidence that a patient “did not try hard enough.” It is a pharmacologic response to physiology and clinical need.

Insulin planning requires attention to formulation, timing, injection technique, meal pattern, glucose monitoring, hypoglycemia education, storage, supplies, cost, caregiver support, and a plan for missed meals or illness. Insulin without education and follow-up is unsafe.

Part 11 — Basal, Prandial, and Correction Logic

Basal insulin addresses background hepatic glucose output. Prandial insulin addresses carbohydrate-related glucose rise. Correction dosing is individualized adjustment for current glucose and trends.

When A1C remains elevated, do not automatically keep increasing basal insulin. Review fasting versus postprandial patterns, hypoglycemia, overnight readings, meal timing, injection technique, adherence, and glucose-monitoring data. “Overbasalization” can create harm if the real issue is postprandial hyperglycemia or a mismatched regimen.

Part 12 — Hypoglycemia Is a Medication-Safety Event

Hypoglycemia can cause adrenergic symptoms such as shakiness, sweating, palpitations, hunger, and anxiety, as well as neuroglycopenic symptoms such as confusion, behavior change, seizure, or loss of consciousness.

Any hypoglycemia episode should trigger a review of timing, food intake, alcohol, activity, insulin or secretagogue use, kidney function, illness, and self-management plan. Severe hypoglycemia, seizure, inability to safely take carbohydrate, altered mental status, or loss of consciousness is an emergency.

Part 13 — Hyperglycemia and Crisis Recognition

Hyperglycemia can lead to polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, weight loss, blurred vision, fatigue, and infection vulnerability. Severe insulin deficiency may lead to DKA; profound dehydration with severe hyperglycemia may lead to hyperosmolar states.

Red flags include vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul-type breathing, confusion, marked weakness, inability to maintain oral hydration, ketone concern, or severe persistent hyperglycemia with illness. Do not manage possible crisis through a routine portal message or delayed outpatient medication adjustment.

Part 14 — Sick-Day Planning

Illness changes glucose, hydration, food intake, insulin requirements, and medication safety. Every patient using insulin or medications with dehydration/ketoacidosis implications needs individualized sick-day instructions.

Key teaching includes more frequent glucose monitoring when directed, hydration, when to check ketones if appropriate, medications that need clinician-directed review during acute illness, and clear thresholds for urgent evaluation. Patients with type 1 diabetes should understand that insulin needs do not disappear simply because oral intake is reduced.

Part 15 — Kidney Disease, Heart Failure, and ASCVD

These comorbidities should actively shape the regimen. Current diabetes standards emphasize selecting medications with demonstrated cardiovascular, kidney, or heart-failure benefit for appropriate patients, independent of A1C in several high-risk contexts.

Translate this into FNP reasoning:

Type 2 diabetes + CKD/HF/ASCVD → assess whether the current plan addresses not only glucose, but also organ-risk reduction, volume status, hypoglycemia risk, and access.

Part 16 — Medication Reconciliation and Devices

Ask about insulin name, concentration, delivery device, timing, dose, needle use, glucose meter or CGM data, test-strip access, recent dose changes, and every noninsulin medication. Insulin errors can occur when products look alike, concentrations are confused, devices are changed, or the prescription and patient’s actual behavior do not match.

Have the patient show or describe how they administer insulin when technique is uncertain. A nonjudgmental demonstration can uncover an error that no laboratory result will reveal.

Part 17 — Clinical Case: Diabetes With HF and CKD

A patient with type 2 diabetes has rising A1C, CKD, and HFrEF with intermittent edema. The medication list includes metformin, a sulfonylurea, a loop diuretic, and a RAAS-active medication.

The FNP-level plan is not just “increase the sulfonylurea.” Consider hypoglycemia risk, kidney function, volume status, heart-failure benefit, current guideline-supported medication options, cost, and a plan to coordinate with cardiology/nephrology when clinically appropriate.

Part 18 — Clinical Case: Nausea on an SGLT2 Inhibitor

A patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, and rapid breathing after a viral illness with poor intake.

Do not reassure based only on a glucose value. Build the mechanism:

Acute illness + reduced intake + susceptible medication context → ketoacidosis risk, including possible euglycemic DKA → urgent evaluation.

Part 19 — Clinical Case: Recurrent Morning Lows

A patient using basal insulin reports waking with sweats and confusion. Their A1C remains above target.

Do not simply increase insulin because the A1C is elevated. Review overnight hypoglycemia, fasting and postmeal patterns, glucose-monitoring data, injection timing, meals, alcohol, kidney function, and the possibility that basal insulin is being used to treat a postprandial problem.

FNP Diabetes Medication Framework

  1. Confirm diabetes type, severity, symptoms, and immediate safety issues.
  2. Set individualized glycemic, weight, cardiovascular, kidney, and hypoglycemia goals.
  3. Select therapy by comorbidities, mechanism, access, adverse effects, and patient preference.
  4. Teach medication use, monitoring, sick-day planning, and red flags.
  5. Reassess glucose data, adverse effects, adherence, technique, and barriers after every change.
  6. Escalate urgently for possible DKA/HHS, severe hypoglycemia, dehydration, or altered mental status.

High-Yield Summary

Metformin: reduces hepatic glucose production; assess tolerance and kidney/acute-illness context.
GLP-1–based therapies: glucose-dependent effects, weight benefit, and selected cardiovascular benefit; assess GI and other safety issues.
SGLT2 inhibitors: glycosuria with selected heart/kidney benefits; assess volume status and ketoacidosis risk.
Sulfonylureas/insulin: effective but higher hypoglycemia risk; reassess when adding other agents.
Insulin: essential in type 1 and sometimes needed in type 2; requires education, monitoring, and a safety plan.
Diabetes pharmacology: treat glucose and organ risk together.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Diabetes medication selection, dosing, titration, insulin adjustments, sick-day instructions, and pregnancy management must follow current guidelines, prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical situation.
